title: Saving the World's Voices
intro: Thousands of languages are in danger of disappearing, but some communities are fighting to keep them alive.

passage: There are around 7,000 languages in the world today, but they are not shared equally. More than half of the world's population speaks just a couple of dozen of them, such as English, Chinese, Hindi and Spanish. At the same time, thousands of languages have only a few hundred speakers, and some have fewer than ten. Experts warn that perhaps 40 per cent of all languages are now endangered, which means they may disappear within the next few generations.

Languages usually die slowly. The process often begins when parents decide that their children will have a better future if they speak the language of the government, schools and business. The children grow up understanding their grandparents' language but rarely using it, and their own children never learn it at all. In the past, some governments even punished pupils for speaking their native language at school. When the last fluent speaker dies, the language is described as extinct.

Why does this matter? Every language contains knowledge that cannot always be translated. Some languages have many precise words for local plants, animals and types of weather, and this information may be useful to scientists. Languages also carry songs, stories and jokes, as well as a particular way of seeing the world. When a language is lost, an important part of a community's identity is often lost with it.

Fortunately, the story does not always end badly. The Isle of Man, a small island between Britain and Ireland, had its own language, Manx. Its last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. Luckily, researchers had recorded him and other elderly speakers years earlier, and enthusiastic learners used these recordings to study the language. Today, a primary school on the island teaches children almost entirely in Manx, and a new generation is growing up with it.

In New Zealand, the Māori language faced a serious decline during the twentieth century. In the 1980s, Māori communities set up “language nests”, where young children spent their days with older people who spoke to them only in Māori. The idea was so successful that it was copied in Hawaii and other places. Similar efforts in Wales, where all pupils now study Welsh at school, show that government support can make a real difference.

Technology is also helping. Linguists use cheap digital recorders to document languages before they vanish, and communities create online dictionaries, mobile apps and even social media groups in their own languages. However, experts agree that recordings alone cannot save a language. A language only survives if people use it every day – at home, with friends and, most importantly, with their children.
